claims.text: The alloy is produced from blended 45–150 μm, 99.9%-pure elemental powders on a Ti6Al4V substrate.
The initial microstructure is approximately 89% BCC A2 with minor BCC B2 and Ti2Ni precipitates.
The initial alloy has an average grain size of 3.66 μm.
The initial alloy has a microhardness of approximately 720 HV.
A 200 W laser with a 3 mm tool offset, 100 mm/min feed rate, and 0.3 mm cutting depth will produce approximately 930 °C at the surface and 800 °C at a depth of 0.3 mm.
Approximately 800 °C lies within this alloy's thermal-softening regime.
Laser preheating temporarily softens the workpiece.
Temporary thermal softening reduces cutting resistance and work hardening.
After removal of the heat-affected surface, laser-assisted machining leaves a layer with a grain size around 3.18 μm.
Laser-assisted machining produces fewer deformation-induced microstructural changes than conventional machining.
Reducing the strength of the preheated cutting region lowers cutting forces and vibration.
Reduced cutting forces and vibration decrease machining-induced work hardening and grain refinement.
Suppressing machining-induced work hardening and grain refinement minimizes detrimental microstructural changes.
After the softened layer is removed, the bulk retains high strength attributable to its fine-grained, predominantly BCC A2 structure and gains improved surface integrity.
Relative to conventional machining, laser-assisted machining will reduce dynamic cutting forces, improve surface roughness, and reduce work hardening.
Laser-assisted machining will preserve a more intact microstructure during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
Laser-assisted machining will produce superior high-temperature tensile properties over 22–1000 °C relative to conventional machining.
Conventional machining produces a more refined grain structure and greater work hardening in the heat-affected zone.
